To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the online correction of visually guided pointing is accomplished by superimposition of dynamically appropriate error correction signals onto the outgoing feed forward motor command to the initial target and that the online correction is proportional to the amplitude and independent of the awareness of the target displacement.

the online correction of visually guided movements can be modeled by a dynamic model of the limb with an error-correction mechanism that superimposes dynamically appropriate error correction signals onto the feedforward motor command and that the mechanism must compensate for the dynamic mechanical characteristics of the limb and the sensory delay in the error-correction pathway.

rapid online corrections are accomplished by superimposition of dynamically appropriate error correction signals onto the feedforward command to the original goal and that the error correction signal must be compensated for both sensory delays and limb dynamics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural control of rapid online corrections to visually guided reaching movements.
the integration of predictive central feedback signals with peripheral sensory feedback signals for the online control of visually-guided movements.

the mechanisms by which humans integrate central and peripheral signals in the control of visually guided limb movements and the role of sensory feedback in the online control of visually directed movements.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human brain uses a dynamic model of the limb to generate an online correction signal for visually guided pointing movements.
the human nervous system uses a dynamic model of the limb in order to predict the future sensory consequences of its own motor command.

the rapid correction of a visually guided movement is accomplished by superimposition of the sensory feedback signal onto a dynamically appropriate error-correction signal, which is generated by a central mechanism and is superimposed onto the feedforward motor command.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the online corrections can be explained by a simple mechanism that is robust to the dynamic mechanical properties and to the sensory delays in its feedback loop.

the human motor system uses a feedforward control strategy to generate a smooth movement to a target and uses an online feedback control strategy to rapidly correct for unexpected target displacements.
the online control mechanism is based on a dynamic model of the limb that is continuously updated by sensory feedback signals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
online correction is a complex process that involves both feedforward and feedback signals and is subject to the dynamic properties of the motor system and sensory delays.

the rapid online correction mechanism can be described as a dynamic model of the limb that is driven by a combination of a feedforward motor command and an error correction signal that is proportional to the error and dynamically appropriate for the limb's dynamics.
the online correction is a fast, dynamic mechanism that is triggered by sensory information regardless of whether the target displacement is detected or not.
